subject: Biology
topic: Food chains and webs — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Organisms that manufacture their own food through photosynthesis are called:
questions.explanation: Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria are producers (autotrophs) — they convert sunlight, CO₂ and water into glucose through photosynthesis. Consumers (heterotrophs) eat producers or other consumers; they include herbivores (cows), carnivores (lions) and omnivores (humans). Decomposers (fungi, bacteria) break down dead matter. Saprophytes specifically feed on dead plant / animal material.

questions.topic: Food chains and webs — mixed tiers

questions.stem: In a typical food chain — grass → grasshopper → frog → snake — the snake occupies which trophic level?
questions.explanation: Trophic levels are counted from the producer upwards: Grass (1st — producer), grasshopper (2nd — primary consumer / herbivore), frog (3rd — secondary consumer / carnivore), snake (4th — tertiary consumer / carnivore). Energy is lost at each level (the 10 % law of Lindeman) — which is why food chains rarely exceed 4-5 links.
questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Food chains and webs — mixed tiers

questions.stem: According to Lindeman's law, the percentage of energy transferred from one trophic level to the next is approximately:
questions.explanation: Only about 10 % of the energy at each level transfers to the next trophic level; the rest is lost as heat (respiration) or stays in the uneaten biomass. This is why food chains are usually short, and why human diets dominated by plant foods are more energy-efficient than meat-heavy ones. Some texts cite 10-20 %, but '10 % rule' is the standard exam answer.

questions.stem: The original source of all energy in most ecosystems is:
questions.explanation: Sunlight is the primary energy source for almost all ecosystems on Earth — captured by producers through photosynthesis and passed along the food chain. Exceptions are deep-sea hydrothermal vent ecosystems that run on chemosynthesis (bacteria using sulphur compounds). Even fossil fuels are, ultimately, stored solar energy from ancient photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead organic matter and return nutrients to the soil are called:
questions.explanation: Decomposers are the recyclers of the ecosystem — without them, dead matter and nutrients would accumulate and plant growth would eventually collapse. They convert complex organic molecules back into inorganic forms (CO₂, nitrates, phosphates) that producers can use. Saprophytes are a subset of decomposers; scavengers (vultures) are different — they eat larger carcasses but do not break them down molecularly.

questions.stem: The phenomenon by which non-biodegradable pollutants (like DDT or mercury) become more concentrated as we move up a food chain is called:
questions.explanation: Biomagnification — successive rise in concentration of a persistent pollutant as it passes up the trophic ladder. Classic example — DDT accumulating in fish-eating birds (ospreys, bald eagles) and causing thin eggshells, highlighted by Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' (1962). Bioaccumulation is buildup within one organism over time; biomagnification is buildup across levels; bioremediation is using organisms to clean pollution.

questions.stem: A 'food web' differs from a 'food chain' because:

options.option_text: It shows the interconnected feeding relationships among many species
It applies only to marine ecosystems

questions.explanation: A food chain is a single linear pathway of who eats whom — grass → deer → tiger. A food web is a network of multiple intersecting chains — e.g., a deer may also be eaten by a leopard or a wild dog, and the grass is also eaten by rabbits. Food webs more accurately represent real ecosystems and their resilience to disturbance. Decomposers are part of any full web.
